strengths: The paper addresses a useful embodied-vision problem: open-vocabulary object navigation without depth or odometry. Integrating target masks into a compact navigation transformer is a practical approach to transferring pretrained visual recognition into navigation.

The complete system reports competitive HM3D-OVON results: 40.1% SR and 20.9% SPL on unseen categories, compared with 18.3% and 7.9% for DAgRL. Its similar seen and unseen success rates are encouraging, and the evaluation includes predicted segmentation rather than relying exclusively on oracle masks.

EALM is simple and implementable. Table 2 supports a modest improvement over DAgRL while using fewer reported training steps: unseen SR increases from 18.3% to 20.2%, and SPL from 7.9% to 8.8%, using 200M rather than 300M steps.

The ablations expose informative tradeoffs, including the large oracle-to-predicted-mask gap, the benefit of filtered-mask adaptation for SPL, and the auxiliary loss's adverse effects on path efficiency and collisions. Architecture details, hyperparameter tables, training curves, and repeated-run statistics provide useful implementation guidance.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol for detector calibration is insufficiently specified and materially affects the main result. Table 4 improves from 35.1% to 40.1% unseen SR after category-specific threshold and vocabulary calibration, while the appendix examines navigation success versus thresholds on the validation splits, including unseen categories. The manuscript does not establish a separate calibration set or explain how thresholds for unseen categories were selected. This leaves potential evaluation-set tuning unresolved; it is not evidence that leakage definitely occurred.

The component ablations do not establish which proposed additions help the deployed system. Table 3 evaluates mask input and the auxiliary loss only with ground-truth masks, whereas replacing oracle masks with YOLOE reduces SR from 70.4% to 35.5%. There is no corresponding predicted-mask ablation removing EALM or the segmentation loss, or comparison against a simpler mask-conditioned policy using the same calibrated detector. Consequently, the contribution beyond adding strong external recognition remains incompletely isolated.

Support for the auxiliary segmentation contribution is mixed. In Table 3 it adds only 1.1 percentage points of SR while reducing SPL from 40.8% to 39.4% and increasing collisions from 14.5 to 18.8. Because the reconstruction target is also supplied as an input, mask reconstruction alone does not demonstrate improved RGB scene understanding or representation disentanglement. A controlled convergence comparison supporting the claimed acceleration is absent.

EALM's description leaves consequential implementation ambiguities. The abstract calls it a per-sample scheduler, but the method describes a minibatch entropy EMA without specifying how sample entropies are aggregated or whether gradients flow through the gate. Fixed entropy bounds replace the switching-time hyperparameter, yet their sensitivity is not evaluated. Table 2 supports lower training cost relative to one baseline, but does not establish a general 33% reduction in sample complexity at matched performance.

Several claims exceed the reported evidence. EALM does not achieve the lowest unseen collision count in Table 2: its 41.8 exceeds EarlySwitcher's 27.7 and DAgger+PPO's 35.8. Raw collisions also depend on episode duration and success, so they do not independently establish safety or diagnose memorization. Table 1 does not support unqualified state-of-the-art SR: MTU3D reports 40.8% versus 40.1%, and the gain over Uni-NaVid is small relative to the reported variability.

Reproducibility and efficiency accounting remain incomplete. The supplied manuscript has no usable code link, does not specify the filtered-mask fine-tuning budget or full category calibration settings, and leaves unclear whether the three seeds represent independent training runs or action-sampling evaluations. The 130M-parameter and low-inference-cost claims lack an explicit accounting of the external segmenter and complete inference latency. These limitations, together with the calibration uncertainty and missing deployed-system ablations, make the current evidence favor weak rejection despite the promising practical results.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: open-vocabulary object navigation with RGB sensing and no depth or odometry. Integrating target masks into a compact temporal policy is practically motivated.

The reported predicted-mask results are competitive. On val unseen, OVSegDT achieves 40.1% SR and 20.9% SPL, compared with 18.3% and 7.9% for DAgRL and 37.1% and 19.8% for DAgRL+OD. These are meaningful improvements over the underlying navigation baseline.

EALM is a simple, implementable approach to mixing imitation and reinforcement learning. Table 2 supports modest improvements over DAgRL with fewer training steps: unseen SR increases from 18.3% to 20.2% using 200M rather than 300M steps.

The experiments distinguish oracle and predicted masks, investigate adaptation to detector errors, and acknowledge the auxiliary loss's performance tradeoffs. The appendix provides hyperparameters, training curves, and statistical comparisons over three runs.
weaknesses: The calibration protocol leaves the central unseen-category result insufficiently validated. Table 4 shows that category-specific detector calibration raises unseen SR from 35.1% to 40.1%, while the appendix examines navigation success versus thresholds for val-unseen categories. The manuscript does not specify an independent calibration set, the selection procedure, or whether evaluation episodes informed these choices. This does not establish leakage, but it prevents assessing whether the headline result represents generalization to unseen goals or adaptation using evaluation feedback.

The ablations do not adequately isolate the proposed contributions in the deployed setting. EALM is compared with other training strategies without masks, whereas the mask and auxiliary-loss ablations use ground-truth segmentation. There is no matched predicted-mask baseline using standard DAgRL training and the same detector calibration, nor a predicted-mask comparison with and without the auxiliary loss. Consequently, the evidence cannot separate the benefits of improved external perception from those of the proposed training components.

The auxiliary objective reconstructs the same current target mask already supplied as input. This can encourage preservation of mask information, but does not by itself demonstrate semantic disentanglement or use of observation history. Its measured benefit is also mixed: Table 3 improves SR from 69.3% to 70.4%, while reducing SPL from 40.8% to 39.4% and increasing collisions from 14.5 to 18.8. The claimed convergence benefit is not isolated by component-specific learning curves.

EALM is described as a per-sample scheduler, but its formulation describes minibatch entropy tracking and an EMA without clearly specifying the reduction or sample-level state. Whether gradients propagate through the entropy-dependent mixing weights is also unspecified and changes the optimization objective. Only one early switching schedule is tested, and sensitivity to the manually chosen entropy bounds is absent, limiting support for the claimed robustness to scheduling choices.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Table 1 reports higher unseen SR for MTU3D (40.8%) than OVSegDT (40.1%), so unqualified state-of-the-art success claims are inaccurate. Table 2 also contradicts the claim that EALM has the lowest collision count: multiple alternatives have fewer collisions. Collision counts per episode are confounded by episode duration and task success; they do not independently establish safer behavior or diagnose trajectory memorization.

Reproducibility and deployment claims remain incomplete. The manuscript does not provide the category-specific calibration settings, precise collision penalty, or adaptation training budget, and the stated code link is blank. It is also unclear whether the 130M-parameter figure includes all inference components, particularly YOLOE, and no full-pipeline latency is reported. Overall, the useful empirical gains warrant consideration, but the unresolved evaluation protocol and contribution-attribution issues currently favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful embodied-vision problem with an RGB-only, mapless policy. Integrating target masks into a compact temporal transformer is a practical way to connect open-vocabulary perception with navigation without requiring depth or odometry.

The reported improvements over DAgRL are substantial: unseen-category SR increases from 18.3% to 40.1%, SPL from 7.9% to 20.9%, and collisions decrease from 50.2 to 24.7 per episode. Even uncalibrated YOLOE masks achieve 35.5% SR, demonstrating value beyond the final calibration procedure.
EALM is simple and implementable. Table 2 supports improved navigation over DAgRL with fewer training steps: unseen SR/SPL increase from 18.3/7.9 to 20.2/8.8 using 200M rather than 300M steps.

The manuscript includes useful component ablations, predicted-versus-oracle mask comparisons, training curves, and three-run statistics. It also explicitly acknowledges the auxiliary loss's tradeoff between success, path efficiency, and collisions.
weaknesses: The calibration protocol leaves the headline unseen-category result difficult to validate. Category-specific detector thresholds and vocabulary changes raise SR from 35.1% to 40.1% in Table 4, while the appendix examines threshold-dependent navigation success on the evaluation splits, including val unseen. The manuscript does not establish which independent data selected these settings or whether evaluation outcomes informed them. This is not proof of leakage, but it materially weakens the evidence for generalization under a fixed deployment procedure.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed components in the deployed setting. Table 3 evaluates the mask encoder and auxiliary loss using ground-truth masks, whereas Table 2 evaluates EALM without masks. There is no predicted-mask comparison with and without EALM or the auxiliary loss under otherwise identical conditions. Consequently, the final gains cannot be attributed confidently to these contributions rather than principally to external detector information and calibration.

Evidence for the auxiliary segmentation contribution is mixed. It improves oracle-mask SR by 1.1 points but reduces SPL from 40.8 to 39.4 and increases collisions from 14.5 to 18.8. Because the reconstruction target is also an input, the objective could primarily encourage preservation of mask information; the stronger claims about semantic disentanglement and faster convergence require evidence beyond this ablation. No auxiliary-loss-specific convergence comparison is provided.

EALM's specification and efficiency claims need tighter support. It is advertised as a per-sample scheduler, but the method describes mini-batch entropy tracking and an EMA without clearly explaining sample-level weighting. The entropy bounds introduce hyperparameters whose sensitivity is not evaluated. Comparing 200M-step EALM against 300M-step DAgRL supports a favorable training-budget comparison, but does not fully establish the claimed reduction in sample complexity at matched performance or account clearly for the subsequent PPO adaptation budget.

Several conclusions overstate the tables. EALM does not achieve the lowest collision count in Table 2; EarlySwitcher and other methods have fewer unseen collisions, although lower success. Raw collisions also depend on episode duration and stopping behavior, so they do not independently establish safety or generalization. Table 1 supports competitive performance and the highest listed unseen SPL, but not the highest unseen SR: MTU3D reports 40.8% versus 40.1%. The 0.6-point SR advantage over Uni-NaVid is not established as statistically reliable.

Reproducibility and deployment-cost reporting remain incomplete despite useful architecture and PPO tables. The supplied manuscript has a blank code link and does not specify the complete calibrated thresholds, vocabulary mapping, fine-tuning duration, or numerical collision penalty. It also lacks end-to-end latency and a clear parameter accounting that includes the external segmentation model. These omissions are secondary to the evaluation concerns, which, together with the missing deployed-setting ablations, make the current balance favor weak rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful embodied vision problem: open-vocabulary object navigation using RGB sensing without depth or odometry. Combining an external open-vocabulary segmenter with a compact history-conditioned policy is a practical approach to transferring semantic recognition into navigation.

The reported HM3D-OVON results are strong. Table 1 reports 44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL on unseen categories, compared with 37.1%/19.8% for DAgRL+OD and 39.5%/19.8% for Uni-NaVid. The similar seen and unseen success rates provide encouraging evidence of category generalization within this benchmark.

The ablations provide meaningful support for combining semantic reward and auxiliary segmentation supervision. In Table 3, the full method achieves 44.7% SR, versus 36.9% without the auxiliary loss and 26.7% without the semantic reward. Table 4 also usefully separates the substantial ground-truth-to-predicted-mask gap from improvements through calibration and policy fine-tuning.

EALM is simple and potentially useful. Table 2 reports improved navigation over DAgRL with 200M rather than 300M training steps. The supplementary material includes threshold sensitivity, training curves, implementation hyperparameters, segmentation failure analysis, and embedded inference measurements. The reported 132 ms latency on Jetson Orin and qualitative robot demonstrations strengthen the practical motivation.
weaknesses: The calibration protocol leaves a material uncertainty about the central unseen-category result. Section 4.3 uses category-specific detector thresholds and vocabulary pruning, while supplementary Section D examines navigation success versus threshold separately on the evaluation splits, explicitly including unseen categories. The manuscript does not specify a disjoint calibration set, the selection procedure, or the final category thresholds. This does not establish evaluation leakage, but it prevents verifying whether the reported unseen performance includes tuning on those categories' evaluation outcomes. Calibration contributes approximately seven SR points, and a fine-tuned policy evaluated with an independently selected global threshold is not reported.

EALM is insufficiently specified to reproduce its claimed per-sample behavior. Equations (5)–(7) combine observation-level entropy, an EMA described as computed for each minibatch, and already averaged PPO/BC losses without explaining whether the gate is global or sample-specific. They also do not state whether gradients flow through the entropy-dependent weights. These choices change the optimization objective. The claimed normalization across action spaces is a heuristic tested only for one six-action setting.

The training comparison does not fully isolate the source of improvement. Table 1 reports an RL baseline with 39.2% seen SR, whereas Table 2's PPO reaches only 7.3%; the relevant differences are not explained. The 33% sample-efficiency claim compares 200M-step EALM against a 300M-step DAgRL result, rather than establishing matched validation learning curves or time to a common performance target. Table 3 also lacks a full mask-based system trained without EALM and a mask-input variant without either auxiliary component, limiting attribution within the final system.

The safety claims exceed the evidence. Predicted-mask fine-tuning raises collisions from 20.2 to 45.4 per episode in Table 4, and the final system's reduction relative to DAgRL is modest. Raw collisions depend on episode duration and success; the discussion divides an overall collision count by a successful-episode length, which does not establish a matched collision rate. The robot demonstrations also report risky behavior near targets. The results support a navigation-performance tradeoff more clearly than broadly safer behavior.

Several interpretive claims need narrower framing. Goal masks, pretrained recognition, transformer policies, semantic rewards, and auxiliary segmentation have precedents acknowledged in the paper, so the novelty primarily lies in their integration and EALM. The complete inference pipeline includes YOLOE and frozen SigLIP encoders, making the end-to-end and 130M-parameter descriptions insufficiently scoped. Free-form language capability is not established; the conclusion explicitly acknowledges this limitation.

The supplementary statistics and segmentation metrics have limitations. The three seeds are described in terms of action sampling, leaving independent training variability unclear. Section H.2's purported pixel-wise FPR/FNR instead classify whole masks using IoU and can count a poorly localized nonempty prediction solely as a false positive, so they do not directly measure conventional pixel-wise over- and under-segmentation. Overall, the substantial empirical gains place this paper near acceptance, but the unresolved calibration protocol and incomplete isolation and specification of the training contribution keep the recommendation borderline.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful embodied-vision problem: open-vocabulary navigation using RGB without depth or odometry. Combining a compact navigation transformer with externally predicted goal masks is practically motivated.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements over DAgRL on unseen categories: SR increases from 18.3% to 44.7%, and SPL from 7.9% to 20.6%. The method also exceeds the listed competitors on this split, although its advantage over Uni-NaVid in SPL is modest.

The adaptation experiments provide meaningful evidence. Table 3 shows that semantic reward and auxiliary segmentation supervision work better together than either individually. Table 4 explicitly measures the large ground-truth-to-predicted-mask gap and the benefits of calibration and fine-tuning.

The supplementary material includes training curves, hyperparameters, failure analysis, photometric robustness experiments, embedded-device timing, and qualitative robot demonstrations. These strengthen the practical contribution beyond a benchmark score alone.
weaknesses: The calibration protocol leaves the central unseen-category result insufficiently established. Section 4.3 uses category-specific detector thresholds and vocabulary pruning, while supplementary Section D examines navigation success versus threshold on the evaluated splits, including val unseen. The manuscript does not specify an independent calibration set, the final category thresholds, or whether unseen-category results use the suggested universal 0.3 threshold. This does not establish evaluation leakage, but it leaves that possibility unresolved. Calibration contributes roughly seven SR points, so the ambiguity materially affects the generalization and state-of-the-art claims.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed architecture and training contributions from stronger external perception. Table 3 lacks a goal-mask-only variant without either auxiliary objective and a mask-equipped DAgRL baseline using the same calibrated YOLOE and adaptation budget. EALM is evaluated separately without masks, but its contribution to the complete system is not isolated. Since prior work already uses detector or mask guidance, these controls are important for assessing the incremental methodological contribution.

EALM's specification and supporting comparisons have consequential gaps. The abstract describes per-sample modulation, whereas Equations 5–7 describe a mini-batch entropy EMA weighting already-averaged losses; reduction and gradient handling are unspecified. Table 2's PPO obtains 0.5% unseen SR, versus 18.6% for the RL baseline in Table 1, without explaining the discrepancy. Comparing 200M EALM steps with 300M DAgRL steps suggests efficiency, but does not cleanly establish the claimed sample-complexity reduction under matched conditions.

The safety claims exceed the evidence. Predicted-mask fine-tuning increases collisions from 20.2 to 45.4 per episode in Table 4. The reported approximately 9% collision rate divides an overall collision count by successful-episode length, which is not a consistently normalized rate. Supplementary Section J also reports risky behavior near real-world goals. The modest reduction against DAgRL is useful, but does not establish broadly safe navigation.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete despite the useful supplement. The collision penalty is unspecified, and it is unclear whether the three seeds represent independent training runs or repeated stochastic evaluations; these support different statistical conclusions. The 130M-parameter claim also needs explicit accounting of the external perception components. These issues are secondary to the calibration and attribution concerns, which determine my weak-reject recommendation despite the promising empirical gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful embodied-vision problem: open-vocabulary object navigation with RGB-only sensing. Integrating goal masks, a temporal transformer, and adaptation to imperfect segmentation provides a practical contribution without requiring depth or odometry at inference.

Table 1 reports strong unseen-category performance: 44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL, compared with 18.3%/7.9% for DAgRL and 39.5%/19.8% for Uni-NaVid. Comparable seen and unseen success rates are encouraging, although the calibration protocol needs clarification.

The ablations support the combined training objectives. In Table 3, semantic reward plus auxiliary segmentation achieves 44.7% unseen SR, versus 36.9% without the auxiliary loss and 26.7% without semantic reward. Table 4 also quantifies the substantial gap between oracle and predicted masks rather than hiding perception limitations.

EALM is a simple, potentially useful training mechanism. Table 2 reports better SR/SPL than DAgRL with 200M rather than 300M training steps. The supplementary threshold study, failure analysis, deployment timings, and qualitative robot demonstrations add useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The main concern is the independence of category-specific calibration from evaluation. Section 4.3 calibrates detector thresholds and edits the vocabulary, while Appendix D examines category-specific navigation success across thresholds on all validation splits, including val unseen. The manuscript does not identify a separate calibration set or clearly specify how thresholds for unseen categories were selected. This does not establish leakage, but leaves the central generalization claim insufficiently verified, particularly because calibration contributes approximately seven SR points. Results for the fully fine-tuned policy with a fixed, independently selected threshold are missing.

Attribution of the full system's gains remains incomplete. Table 3 lacks a goal-mask-only variant without either auxiliary objective and a full-system variant trained without EALM. Thus, the experiments support the combined system more strongly than the necessity of each proposed component. The architecture largely extends an existing navigation transformer with established mask encoding and segmentation supervision, making controlled attribution especially important.

EALM's implementation is underspecified: it is described as per-sample modulation, but Equations 5–7 describe a minibatch entropy EMA multiplying already-averaged losses. The reduction, EMA indexing, and whether gradients pass through the gate are unclear. Threshold sensitivity is investigated, but generalization of the proposed entropy rule across action spaces is asserted without corresponding experiments. The additional predicted-mask fine-tuning stage also qualifies the broad single-stage-training claim.

The safety evidence is mixed. Table 4 shows collisions increasing from 20.2 to 45.4 per episode after predicted-mask fine-tuning, and Appendix J acknowledges risky behavior near real goals. The final model improves modestly over DAgRL's 50.2 collisions, but episode-level counts confound safety with duration and termination behavior. Dividing aggregate collisions by successful-episode length does not resolve this.

Reproducibility and claim precision need improvement. It is unclear whether the three seeds represent independent training runs or action-sampling evaluations. The collision penalty and complete calibration settings are not specified. The headline parameter count lacks a clear accounting of all perception modules, and Appendix J provides demonstrations rather than a quantitative robot evaluation. Separately, the GPU-memory units in Table J are evidently erroneous. Overall, the promising empirical contribution is balanced by unresolved evaluation-protocol and attribution concerns, placing the paper at the decision boundary.
